bases.narrative: My mother can't manage on her own any more, and my brother and I are deciding together what to do; it is our decision to make, with Mom's blessing. Her doctor says she can live safely at home with a daytime aide, or she can move into Maple Court, an assisted-living facility. Maple Court charges $6,200 a month. Mom's long-term-care insurance pays $1,500 a month toward a facility but nothing toward home care. An aide would work 30 hours a week at $40 an hour, and we count a month as 52/12 weeks. Maple Court is a six-minute drive from my apartment; Mom's house is about 35 minutes from me. Our rule: we will move Mom into Maple Court if and only if its monthly cost after her insurance pays its share is lower than the aide's monthly cost; otherwise we will hire the aide. Nothing else is part of this decision for us.
bases.question: Should we move Mom into Maple Court or hire an aide?

options.text: Hire a daytime aide so Mom stays at home

bases.narrative: Our furnace is 17 years old and needs work, and my wife and I make this decision together. The repair quote is $3,900. A heat pump is quoted at $13,800 installed, and the state rebate for our county is $3,000. The installer says the heat pump would cut our heating bill by about $70 a month. Our rule: we will replace the furnace with a heat pump if and only if the installed price minus the rebate comes to less than $12,000; at $12,000 or more we will repair the furnace. Nothing else enters this decision for us.
bases.question: Should we install the heat pump or repair the furnace?

bases.narrative: My partner and I are choosing childcare for our daughter, and the choice is ours together. Little Oaks daycare costs $1,850 a month and runs 7:30 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., with 12 children in her room. Our half of a nanny share would be $2,050 a month, from 8:00 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., with two children. Our rule: we will go with the nanny share if and only if our half costs no more than $300 a month above Little Oaks; otherwise we will choose Little Oaks. Nothing else decides it for us.

bases.narrative: My husband and I are choosing a kindergarten for our daughter Priya; the decision is ours. The district's route sheet puts the bus ride to Ridgeview Magnet at 50 minutes each way. bases.narrative: My partner and I are deciding whether to put solar panels on our house; it's a joint decision. The installer quotes $21,000, and the federal tax credit covers 30% of that. The panels would save us about $1,500 a year on electricity. We expect to stay in this house about 12 more years. The roof was replaced 6 years ago. Our rule: we will install solar if and only if the cost after the tax credit, divided by the yearly savings, comes to fewer years than we expect to stay; otherwise we skip it. Nothing else counts in this choice for us.

bases.narrative: I'm deciding how to get to work for the next two years, and it's my call alone. The e-bike I want costs $2,400, and upkeep runs about $300 a year.
